name: Tonsil stone removal

lead: Tonsil stones (tonsilloliths) are hardened clumps of debris, dead cells and bacteria that form in the crevices of the tonsils. Many people have no symptoms, but bad breath is the most commonly reported complaint, and removal is a frequent topic in breath-focused looksmaxxing discussion.

Options described in medical references range from salt-water gargling and gentle swabbing to dentist or ENT removal, laser smoothing of the tonsil surface (cryptolysis) and, rarely, tonsillectomy. Rigorous trials comparing these options are scarce.

paras: Stones sit in tonsil crypts and contain bacterial biofilm and calcium salts. Removing them clears a source of odour-producing bacteria; reshaping the crypts with a laser aims to make re-collection less likely.

Gentle home approaches are described as low risk, but high-pressure irrigators can tear tonsil tissue and cause infection. Stones often recur, and large stones can be mistaken for abscesses or tumours, so persistent symptoms are generally assessed by a clinician.

lead: Tonsil stones, or tonsilloliths, are mineralised accumulations of debris in the crypts of the tonsils, most often the palatine tonsils. The unmineralised form is called chronic caseous tonsillitis. Wikipedia reports that stones contain bacterial biofilm and calcium salts, with aerobic bacteria on the surface and anaerobes at the core, and that up to about 10 percent of people may have them [1].

Bad breath is the most common complaint, although many people have no symptoms and stones are sometimes found incidentally on imaging [1]. Wikipedia cites a 2007 study finding tonsilloliths in 75 percent of patients with bad breath and 6 percent of those with normal breath [1]. Overall, most halitosis is reported to originate in the mouth itself, mainly on the back of the tongue, with the tonsils estimated as a minor contributor in some reports and a more important one in others [2].

Approaches described for removal include warm salt-water gargling, cotton swab or low-pressure irrigation, antibacterial rinses, clinician curettage, laser cryptolysis and tonsillectomy [1]. No published randomised trials were found comparing these approaches for bad breath.

paras: Stones form when debris such as dead cells, mucus and bacteria becomes trapped in the tonsil crypts and hardens, often in people with recurrent tonsillitis or chronic tonsil inflammation; the exact mechanism is described as still debated [1]. Most stones are small, but ones weighing from 0.3 g up to 42 g have been recorded [1]. Symptoms besides bad breath include sore throat, a feeling of something stuck, pain on swallowing, cough, earache and a metallic taste [1].

Wikipedia notes that stones are usually benign and need no treatment if they cause no problems. Home options listed are warm salt-water gargling, removing stones with a cotton swab and low-pressure oral irrigators, while powerful electric irrigators can rupture the tonsils and cause infection [1]. Chlorhexidine or cetylpyridinium chloride rinses may be tried [1].

Larger stones may be removed by clinician curettage followed by irrigation. Laser cryptolysis uses a carbon dioxide laser under local anaesthetic to smooth the tonsil surface so debris is less likely to be trapped, and partial or complete tonsillectomy may be considered if bad breath persists or complications occur [1]. Wikipedia's tonsillectomy article states that there is no good evidence supporting tonsillectomy for tonsil stones or bad breath [3].

Reported complications include recurrent bad breath that curettage or laser may not fully resolve, rare need for surgical extraction, infection after overly forceful irrigation, and misdiagnosis, since giant tonsilloliths can be mistaken for peritonsillar abscesses or tumours [1].

No randomised trials of home or clinic stone removal for bad breath were found. Published literature cited by Wikipedia consists mainly of case reports and reviews, including a 2009 study showing tonsilloliths contain living biofilm, a 2014 review on management of tonsil-related halitosis by Ferguson and colleagues, and a 2015 description of stones as polymicrobial biofilms [1]. A 2019 Cochrane review of halitosis interventions, cited by Wikipedia, found no strong evidence on which interventions work best [2].
